cards.q: In sensory physiology, what does transduction mean?
cards.a: Conversion of stimulus energy into a change in membrane potential.
options: Conversion of stimulus energy into a change in membrane potential
Propagation of an action potential along a sensory axon toward the cord
Release of neurotransmitter onto a second order neuron
Amplification of a weak signal by the somatosensory cortex
cards.explanation: Transduction happens at the receptor membrane, where pressure, light, heat, or a chemical opens or closes ion channels and changes the voltage across that membrane. Propagation comes later, after the graded potential reaches the trigger zone. Transmitter release is the synaptic handoff further along the pathway, and cortical processing is central, not a receptor event.

cards.q: How does the size of a receptor potential change as the stimulus gets stronger?
cards.a: It gets larger in proportion to the stimulus.
options: It stays fixed, because the response is all or none
It gets larger in proportion to the stimulus
It gets smaller as the receptor is loaded
It stays flat until threshold and then jumps
cards.explanation: Receptor potentials are graded: a stronger stimulus opens more channels and produces a larger depolarization. All or none describes the action potential, not the receptor potential. Nothing about a stronger stimulus shrinks the response, and the sudden jump at threshold belongs to the trigger zone, not to the graded potential itself.

cards.q: In most somatosensory receptors, which ion movement produces the depolarizing receptor potential?
cards.a: Na+ moving into the cell.
options: K+ moving out of the cell
Cl- moving into the cell
Ca2+ being pumped out of the cell
Na+ moving into the cell
cards.explanation: Stimulus energy opens nonselective cation channels, and because the electrochemical gradient for Na+ is large and inward, Na+ entry dominates and depolarizes the ending. K+ leaving and Cl- entering both drive the membrane away from threshold, so they hyperpolarize instead. Pumping Ca2+ out is a recovery process and carries no significant part of the receptor potential.

cards.q: In a myelinated sensory neuron, where is the receptor potential first converted into action potentials?
cards.a: At the trigger zone near the first node of Ranvier.
options: At the receptor membrane where the stimulus lands
At the axon terminal inside the spinal cord
At the trigger zone near the first node of Ranvier
At the cell body in the dorsal root ganglion
cards.explanation: The receptor membrane carries few voltage gated Na+ channels, so it can only make a graded potential. That potential spreads a short distance to the trigger zone, the first node of Ranvier, where voltage gated Na+ channels are dense enough to fire. The terminal in the cord is where the message is handed to the next neuron, and the dorsal root ganglion cell body sits off to the side of the conducting axon.

cards.q: Which property belongs to the receptor potential but not to the action potential?
cards.a: It is graded and decays as it spreads.
options: It is all or none once threshold is reached
It has an absolute refractory period
It is produced only by voltage gated Na+ channels
It is graded and decays as it spreads
cards.explanation: A receptor potential varies in size with the stimulus and loses amplitude as it spreads passively along the membrane. All or none behavior, a refractory period, and dependence on voltage gated Na+ channels are all features of the action potential, which is regenerated at full size at every node. That difference is exactly why the receptor potential cannot travel to the spinal cord by itself.

cards.q: What does the adequate stimulus of a receptor describe?
cards.a: The form of energy the receptor responds to at the lowest intensity.
options: The smallest stimulus that produces a detectable receptor potential
The form of energy the receptor responds to at the lowest intensity
The stimulus strength that drives the receptor to its maximum firing rate
The stimulus duration needed to keep the receptor from adapting
cards.explanation: Each receptor is tuned to one kind of energy, and the adequate stimulus names that kind. A photoreceptor can be fired by a hard blow to the eye, but light is its adequate stimulus because far less energy is needed. The smallest detectable stimulus is the threshold, the strength that maxes out firing is saturation, and adaptation is a separate property.

cards.q: In a sensory neuron whose own bare ending is the receptor, the graded depolarization produced by the stimulus is called what?
cards.a: A generator potential.
options: A generator potential
An end plate potential
An excitatory postsynaptic potential
An after hyperpolarization
cards.explanation: When the receptor and the action potential generating neuron are the same cell, the receptor potential is called a generator potential because it directly generates the train of action potentials. An end plate potential is the graded potential at the neuromuscular junction, and an excitatory postsynaptic potential is produced by transmitter at a synapse. An after hyperpolarization follows an action potential rather than causing one.

cards.q: Once a sensory neuron is firing, what happens to the amplitude of its action potentials as the stimulus grows stronger?
cards.a: It stays the same.
options: It rises with stimulus strength
It falls as the neuron fatigues
It doubles once threshold is passed
It stays the same
cards.explanation: Action potentials are all or none, so their height is set by the Na+ and K+ gradients and not by the stimulus. Stimulus strength is carried in the firing rate instead. The receptor potential is the part of the system that grows with stimulus strength, which is a common place to mix the two up.

cards.q: A pressure stimulus on the skin doubles in strength. What changes in the sensory axon?
cards.a: The action potentials come at a higher frequency.
options: The action potentials come at a higher frequency
The action potentials become taller
The action potentials travel faster along the axon
The action potentials last longer in duration
cards.explanation: A stronger stimulus makes a larger receptor potential, which drives the trigger zone back to threshold sooner after each spike, so spikes come closer together. Height is fixed by the all or none rule, and both conduction velocity and spike duration are set by axon diameter, myelination, and channel kinetics, not by how hard the skin is pressed.

cards.q: A very light touch produces a receptor potential that does not reach threshold at the trigger zone. What does the sensory axon do?
cards.a: It fires no action potentials, though a graded potential is present.
options: It fires one small action potential
It fires at a low but steady frequency for as long as the touch lasts
It fires no action potentials, though a graded potential is present
It fires a burst only when the touch is removed
cards.explanation: Transduction still happened, so a graded depolarization sits at the ending, but without reaching threshold the trigger zone opens no voltage gated Na+ channels in a regenerative way and nothing is sent. There is no such thing as a small action potential, since spikes are all or none. Firing at a low rate would require threshold to be crossed, and an off response belongs to certain phasic receptors, not to a subthreshold stimulus.

cards.q: A toxin blocks the mechanically gated channels of a Pacinian corpuscle but leaves every other channel working. What happens when the skin is pressed?
cards.a: No receptor potential forms, so no action potentials are fired.
options: A receptor potential forms but no action potentials follow
No receptor potential forms, so no action potentials are fired
A normal receptor potential and a normal train of action potentials occur
A hyperpolarizing receptor potential forms and firing slows
cards.explanation: Blocking the mechanically gated channels removes the first step, so pressure never changes the membrane voltage and there is nothing to spread to the trigger zone. A receptor potential with no spikes is what you would see if the block were on the voltage gated Na+ channels at the trigger zone instead. Normal responses require intact transduction, and a hyperpolarization would require an outward current the toxin does not create.

cards.q: Rod photoreceptors respond to light by hyperpolarizing rather than depolarizing. What does that tell you about receptor potentials in general?
cards.a: A receptor potential can be a depolarization or a hyperpolarization.
options: Receptor potentials must always be depolarizations
Photoreceptors skip transduction and fire action potentials directly
Hyperpolarization means the light was below threshold
A receptor potential can be a depolarization or a hyperpolarization
cards.explanation: A receptor potential is simply the voltage change the stimulus produces, and its direction depends on which channels the stimulus controls. Light closes cation channels in rods, so the membrane hyperpolarizes and the cell releases less transmitter, which is still a signal. Rods do transduce, they just do not fire action potentials, and the hyperpolarization is the response itself rather than a sign that the stimulus was too weak.

cards.q: A sensory neuron is firing at its maximum rate, and further increases in stimulus strength do not raise that rate. What sets the ceiling?
cards.a: The absolute refractory period of the axon.
options: The absolute refractory period of the axon
The size of the receptor potential
The number of mechanically gated channels in the ending
The conduction velocity of the axon
cards.explanation: During the absolute refractory period the voltage gated Na+ channels are inactivated and no stimulus of any size can produce another spike, so the refractory period puts a hard ceiling on frequency. The receptor potential and channel number set how quickly the neuron climbs toward that ceiling, not where the ceiling sits. Conduction velocity governs how fast a spike travels, not how often one can be launched.

cards.q: Two weak taps, each too small to reach threshold alone, arrive at a receptor a few milliseconds apart and together trigger an action potential. Why?
cards.a: Their graded receptor potentials sum before either has decayed.
options: Each tap becomes all or none when it is repeated
The second tap lowers the threshold at the trigger zone
Their graded receptor potentials sum before either has decayed
The first tap leaves a refractory period that adds to the second
cards.explanation: Graded potentials can add together, so if the second arrives before the first has faded the two depolarizations combine and the total can cross threshold. Repetition does not convert a graded potential into an all or none one, and threshold at the trigger zone is set by channel properties rather than by the previous stimulus. A refractory period makes firing harder, not easier.

cards.q: Why can a receptor potential not carry touch information from the fingertip all the way to the spinal cord?
cards.a: It decays with distance, while action potentials are regenerated.
options: It travels too slowly to be useful over a distance that long
It decays with distance, while action potentials are regenerated
It is blocked by the myelin sheath along the axon
It is too large to pass through the dorsal root ganglion cell body
cards.explanation: Graded potentials spread passively and lose amplitude with every micrometer, so over a meter of arm nothing would be left. The action potential solves this by being rebuilt at full height at each node of Ranvier. Speed is not the limiting problem, myelin speeds passive spread rather than blocking it, and amplitude is not what a ganglion filters.

cards.q: A local anesthetic is applied at the trigger zone of a touch receptor and blocks the voltage gated Na+ channels there. The mechanically gated channels in the ending are untouched. What happens when the skin is pressed?
cards.a: A normal receptor potential forms, but no action potentials are fired.
options: A normal receptor potential forms, but no action potentials are fired
Neither a receptor potential nor an action potential occurs
A receptor potential forms and a normal train of action potentials follows
The receptor potential reverses to a hyperpolarization
cards.explanation: Transduction is intact, so pressure still opens the mechanically gated channels and still produces a graded depolarization that spreads to the trigger zone. What is missing is the regenerative step, because blocked voltage gated Na+ channels cannot convert that depolarization into spikes, and the patient feels nothing. Losing the receptor potential as well would require blocking the transduction channels, and nothing here creates an outward current to reverse the potential.

cards.q: A toxin locks the mechanically gated channels of a touch receptor open, so the ending sits strongly depolarized even with no stimulus. What is the most likely effect on that neuron?
cards.a: It fires at rest and reports added pressure poorly, since the trigger zone is inactivated.
options: It goes silent from the start, because a steady depolarization cannot by itself trigger any firing
It fires at rest and reports added pressure poorly, since the trigger zone is inactivated
It responds normally, but only while the skin is being pressed
It hyperpolarizes and fires a rebound burst when pressure is applied
cards.explanation: A maintained depolarization first drives firing, so the neuron reports touch that is not there, and it also holds many voltage gated Na+ channels in the inactivated state, so an actual press adds little extra firing and the useful range is lost. Steady depolarization does trigger firing at first rather than silencing the cell outright. Normal responsiveness would require a normal resting voltage, and nothing in this scenario produces a hyperpolarization.

cards.q: Two touch receptors receive identical pressure. Receptor A has twice as many mechanically gated channels in its ending as receptor B, and their trigger zones are identical. What should a recording show?
cards.a: Receptor A has the larger receptor potential and fires at the higher frequency.
options: Receptor A has a larger receptor potential but the same firing frequency
Both receptor potentials are the same size, but A fires taller action potentials
Receptor A has the larger receptor potential and fires at the higher frequency
Receptor B has the larger receptor potential because it has fewer channels to share the current
cards.explanation: More transduction channels means more inward current for the same pressure, a bigger graded depolarization, and a trigger zone that returns to threshold sooner after each spike, so both the receptor potential and the firing rate go up. Firing rate cannot stay flat while the receptor potential grows, because rate is what the graded potential controls. Spike height is fixed by the all or none rule, and fewer channels carry less current, not more.

cards.q: A recording shows a steady 15 mV graded depolarization at a sensory ending but no action potentials in its axon, even though that axon conducts normally when stimulated directly with an electrode. Where is the failure?
cards.a: In the spread of the graded potential to the trigger zone, which never reaches threshold.
options: In the mechanically gated channels of the ending, which are apparently not opening at all
In the spread of the graded potential to the trigger zone, which never reaches threshold
In the axon membrane, which can no longer conduct
In the synapse onto the second order neuron in the cord
cards.explanation: Two facts bracket the problem: transduction works, since a 15 mV receptor potential is present, and conduction works, since direct stimulation produces spikes. That leaves the step between them, where the graded potential must spread to the trigger zone and reach threshold, and 15 mV at the ending can decay to less than that on the way. A transduction failure would show no receptor potential, a conduction failure would block the electrode test as well, and a synaptic failure would be invisible in a recording from this axon.

cards.q: What kind of stimulus does a mechanoreceptor transduce?
cards.a: Physical deformation such as pressure, stretch, or vibration.
options: A change in local temperature
A change in the concentration of a dissolved chemical in the tissue
Physical deformation such as pressure, stretch, or vibration
Tissue damage severe enough to be felt as pain
cards.explanation: Mechanoreceptors have channels that open when the membrane is physically pulled or pushed, so pressure, stretch, and vibration are all adequate stimuli for them. Temperature is the domain of thermoreceptors, dissolved molecules of chemoreceptors, and damaging stimuli of nociceptors. Classification is always by the form of energy the receptor is tuned to, not by where in the body it sits.

cards.q: What kind of stimulus does a chemoreceptor transduce?
cards.a: The concentration of a chemical such as O2, H+, or a nutrient.
options: The concentration of a chemical such as O2, H+, or a nutrient
The stretch of a vessel wall as blood pressure rises inside it
The wavelength of light striking a pigment
The rate at which local tissue is warming
cards.explanation: Chemoreceptors bind or respond to molecules and ions, which is why taste, smell, blood gases, and blood pH all run through them. Vessel wall stretch is sensed by mechanoreceptors even though the trigger is blood pressure, light by photoreceptors, and warming by thermoreceptors. The chemical itself, not the consequence, is what defines the class.

cards.q: What kind of stimulus does a thermoreceptor transduce?
cards.a: A change in temperature of the tissue around the ending.
options: The pressure of an object resting on the skin
The presence of a damaging chemical released in the tissue
The stretch of skin as a joint is moved
A change in temperature of the tissue around the ending
cards.explanation: Thermoreceptors carry channels whose opening probability depends on temperature, and separate populations report cooling and warming. Pressure and skin stretch are mechanical and belong to mechanoreceptors, while a damaging chemical activates nociceptors. Note that very hot or very cold temperatures also recruit nociceptors, which is why extreme temperature is felt as pain rather than as temperature alone.

cards.q: What defines a nociceptor?
cards.a: It responds to stimuli intense enough to damage tissue.
options: It responds only to chemicals released by immune cells
It responds to stimuli intense enough to damage tissue
It responds to any stimulus once the person reports discomfort
It responds only to mechanical stimuli above a set force
cards.explanation: A nociceptor is defined by the intensity and threat of the stimulus rather than by its form, which is why heat above about 45 C, crushing pressure, and acid can all activate the same ending. Inflammatory chemicals sensitize nociceptors but are not the only trigger. The definition rests on the stimulus, not on the person's report, and it is not limited to mechanical energy.

cards.q: Where in the body are photoreceptors found?
cards.a: In the retina at the back of the eye.
options: In the cornea at the front of the eye
In the optic nerve behind the globe
In the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
In the retina at the back of the eye
cards.explanation: Rods and cones sit in the retina, which is the only tissue in the body with the pigment needed to transduce light. The cornea contains no photoreceptors and is instead densely supplied with nociceptors, which is why a scratch on it hurts so much. The optic nerve and the lateral geniculate carry and relay the already transduced signal rather than transducing light themselves.

cards.q: The carotid bodies monitor arterial PO2, PCO2, and pH. Which receptor class do they belong to?
cards.a: Chemoreceptors.
options: Chemoreceptors
Mechanoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
Nociceptors
cards.explanation: The stimulus is the concentration of dissolved gases and H+, so these are chemoreceptors, sitting at the fork of the common carotid artery. It is easy to confuse them with the carotid sinus baroreceptors right next door, which respond to stretch and are mechanoreceptors. Neither temperature nor tissue damage is the adequate stimulus at this site.

cards.q: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus fire when arterial pressure rises. Which receptor class are they?
cards.a: Mechanoreceptors.
options: Chemoreceptors
Nociceptors
Mechanoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
cards.explanation: Pressure is detected indirectly here: rising pressure stretches the vessel wall, the ending is deformed, and mechanically gated channels open, so baroreceptors are mechanoreceptors. The name points to what is being measured, not to the energy being transduced, which is a common trap. Chemoreceptors at the nearby carotid body respond to blood chemistry instead, and neither temperature nor damage is involved.

cards.q: Which structure serves as the sensory ending for most nociceptors and thermoreceptors in the skin?
cards.a: Free nerve endings.
options: Pacinian corpuscles
Free nerve endings
Muscle spindles
Meissner corpuscles
cards.explanation: Pain and temperature are carried by bare, unencapsulated terminals of small diameter fibers, which is why these two modalities travel together in the same fiber classes and the same pathway. Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles are encapsulated mechanoreceptors tuned to vibration and light touch, and muscle spindles are stretch mechanoreceptors inside muscle. The capsule is what filters mechanical energy, and pain endings do without one.

cards.q: Hair cells in the cochlea are bent by fluid movement set up by sound waves. How should they be classified?
cards.a: As mechanoreceptors.
options: As mechanoreceptors
As chemoreceptors
As photoreceptors
As nociceptors
cards.explanation: Sound reaches the hair cell as physical motion of fluid and membrane, and bending the stereocilia pulls open mechanically gated channels, so the adequate stimulus is deformation. Classify by the energy the receptor actually transduces, not by the everyday name of the sense. The chemical synapse the hair cell makes onto the auditory nerve comes after transduction and does not make it a chemoreceptor.

cards.q: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus fire when plasma osmolarity rises. What are they responding to?
cards.a: Cell shrinkage, which deforms the membrane and opens ion channels.
options: The temperature of the blood perfusing the hypothalamus
Damage to the neurons caused by concentrated plasma
Light reaching the hypothalamus through the retinohypothalamic tract
Cell shrinkage, which deforms the membrane and opens ion channels
cards.explanation: When osmolarity rises, water leaves the osmoreceptor cell, the cell shrinks, and the membrane deformation opens mechanically gated channels, so the transduction step is mechanical even though the variable being monitored is chemical. This is the same lesson as the baroreceptor: the measured quantity and the transduced energy can differ. No damage, temperature change, or light is involved in the response.

cards.q: Capsaicin, the compound in chili peppers, opens the same channel that noxious heat opens. What does eating a hot pepper therefore feel like?
cards.a: Burning heat and pain, because nociceptors are activated by the chemical.
options: Cooling, because the channel is a cold sensing channel
Burning heat and pain, because nociceptors are activated by the chemical
Nothing at all, because chemicals cannot activate a heat sensitive channel
Pressure, because the channel is mechanically gated
cards.explanation: The TRPV1 channel opens either at temperatures above roughly 43 C or when capsaicin binds it, and the brain reads any traffic on that line as burning heat and pain. This shows that a nociceptor can be polymodal, responding to chemical and thermal energy through one channel. Menthol produces the mirror image effect on a cold sensitive channel, and neither channel is gated by pressure.

cards.q: Muscle spindles fire when a muscle is stretched, reporting muscle length to the CNS. Which class do they belong to?
cards.a: Mechanoreceptors.
options: Chemoreceptors
Nociceptors
Mechanoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
cards.explanation: Stretch deforms the spindle ending and opens mechanically gated channels, so the spindle is a mechanoreceptor even though it lies deep in muscle rather than in skin. Location does not determine class. Muscle also contains chemoreceptors that report metabolites and nociceptors that report damage, so all three classes share the tissue but respond to different energies.

cards.q: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla drive breathing when arterial PCO2 rises. What do they actually sense?
cards.a: H+ in the cerebrospinal fluid, which rises as CO2 diffuses in.
options: H+ in the cerebrospinal fluid, which rises as CO2 diffuses in
Stretch of the medullary blood vessels as CO2 dilates them
The temperature of the brainstem, which CO2 raises
The direct binding of CO2 to a receptor protein on the neuron membrane
cards.explanation: CO2 crosses the blood brain barrier easily, combines with water to form carbonic acid, and lowers cerebrospinal fluid pH, and it is that H+ change the central chemoreceptors detect. This is why they respond to a rise in PCO2 quickly but to a metabolic acidosis in the blood only slowly, since H+ itself crosses the barrier poorly. Vessel stretch, temperature, and direct CO2 binding are not the transduction step here.

cards.q: Taste receptor cells in the tongue respond to molecules dissolved in saliva. Which class are they, and where is the matching class found in the airway control system?
cards.a: Chemoreceptors, matched by the carotid and aortic bodies.
options: Mechanoreceptors, matched by the airway stretch receptors
Thermoreceptors, matched by the hypothalamic warm cells
Nociceptors, matched by the free nerve endings in the trachea
Chemoreceptors, matched by the carotid and aortic bodies
cards.explanation: Taste depends on molecules binding receptor proteins on the taste cell, which makes it a chemoreceptor, and the peripheral chemoreceptors of the carotid and aortic bodies use the same class to monitor blood gases. Airway stretch receptors are mechanoreceptors, the hypothalamic cells are thermoreceptors, and tracheal free nerve endings are nociceptors, all real receptors but not the same class as taste.

cards.q: A person steps barefoot on a tack. Which receptor class is activated by the puncture itself?
cards.a: Nociceptors.
options: Photoreceptors
Nociceptors
Chemoreceptors
Thermoreceptors
cards.explanation: A puncture is mechanical energy at a damaging intensity, and that is exactly the definition of a nociceptor stimulus, so the high threshold free nerve endings fire. Low threshold mechanoreceptors in the sole also fire, which is why the foot is felt as well as hurt, but they are not what makes it painful. Chemoreceptors join in a few seconds later as damaged cells release K+ and bradykinin, and temperature and light play no part.

cards.q: After a spinal cord injury a patient has lost pain and temperature sensation in the legs but still feels light touch and vibration normally. What does this tell you about the receptors and fibers involved?
cards.a: Pain and temperature share small fibers and a pathway separate from touch.
options: Nociceptors and thermoreceptors were destroyed in the skin itself
Touch receptors must also transduce temperature, so they compensated
Pain and temperature share small fibers and a pathway separate from touch
Thermoreceptors are a subtype of nociceptor, so the two must always fail together
cards.explanation: Free nerve endings for pain and temperature feed thin A delta and C fibers that cross and ascend in the spinothalamic tract, while encapsulated touch and vibration receptors feed large myelinated fibers in the dorsal columns, so a cord lesion can take one and spare the other. The skin receptors themselves are intact, since the injury is central. Touch receptors do not transduce temperature, and thermoreceptors are a distinct class from nociceptors even though they travel together.

cards.q: A patient's blood pressure falls sharply and, at the same time, arterial PO2 drops. Two receptor populations only millimeters apart in the neck respond. Which is which?
cards.a: The carotid sinus mechanoreceptors report the pressure fall and the carotid body chemoreceptors report the PO2 fall.
options: The carotid sinus mechanoreceptors report the pressure fall and the carotid body chemoreceptors report the PO2 fall
The carotid sinus chemoreceptors report the pressure fall and the carotid body mechanoreceptors report the PO2 fall
Both sites are chemoreceptors and both respond to the PO2 fall
Both sites are mechanoreceptors and both respond to the pressure fall
cards.explanation: The carotid sinus is a stretch sensitive segment of arterial wall, so falling pressure unloads it and it fires less, which is a mechanoreceptor response. The carotid body is a small chemosensitive organ next to it that fires more as PO2 falls, which is a chemoreceptor response. The names are similar and the sites are adjacent, but the adequate stimuli are different, and neither site can substitute for the other.

cards.q: A single free nerve ending is recorded and found to fire to a pinch, to heat above 45 C, and to acid applied to the skin, but not to a light brush. How is this ending best classified?
cards.a: As a polymodal nociceptor, since every effective stimulus is damaging.
options: As a mechanoreceptor, since pinch was one of the stimuli
As a thermoreceptor, since heat was one of the stimuli
As three separate receptors that happened to be recorded together by accident
As a polymodal nociceptor, since every effective stimulus is damaging
cards.explanation: The pattern is the giveaway: the ending ignores gentle mechanical stimulation but responds to mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli once they reach tissue damaging levels, which is the signature of a polymodal nociceptor. Calling it a mechanoreceptor or thermoreceptor picks one stimulus and ignores the threshold, and low threshold receptors of those classes would have responded to the light brush. A single recorded ending is one receptor, and polymodal responses are its normal behavior.

cards.q: A newly described ending in the stomach wall fires when the stomach is distended and also when luminal pH falls, but is silent to warming and to gentle stroking. Which two classes best describe it?
cards.a: A mechanoreceptor response to distension and a chemoreceptor response to acid.
options: A thermoreceptor response to distension and a nociceptor response to acid
A mechanoreceptor response to distension and a chemoreceptor response to acid
A chemoreceptor response to distension and a mechanoreceptor response to acid
A photoreceptor response to distension and a thermoreceptor response to acid
cards.explanation: Distension stretches the wall, which is deformation and therefore a mechanoreceptor response, while a fall in pH is a change in H+ concentration, which is a chemoreceptor response. Matching each stimulus to the energy it carries is the whole skill here, so pairing distension with chemistry or acid with deformation reverses the logic. Silence to warming rules out a thermoreceptor role, and there is no light in the stomach for a photoreceptor to transduce.

cards.q: In sensory coding, what does the term modality refer to?
cards.a: The type of sensation, such as touch, cold, or pain.
options: The strength of the sensation the person reports
The type of sensation, such as touch, cold, or pain
The part of the body where the sensation is felt
The length of time the sensation lasts
cards.explanation: Modality is the what of a stimulus, the qualitative category the brain assigns it, and it is set by which pathway carries the signal. Strength is intensity, place is location, and length is duration, and the nervous system codes each of those four features by a different means. Keeping the four straight is the whole point of this competency.

cards.q: What does the labeled line principle state?
cards.a: Each pathway carries one modality, and the brain reads it from which pathway is active.
options: Each pathway carries one modality, and the brain reads it from which pathway is active
Each pathway can carry any modality, and the modality is coded in the pattern of spikes
Each pathway carries a single body region, and the modality is decided in the cortex
Each pathway carries one intensity level, and stronger stimuli use different lines
cards.explanation: Action potentials look the same in every sensory neuron, so the only way the brain can tell cold from pressure is by knowing which line the traffic arrived on, and that line is labeled by where it terminates centrally. Modality is therefore not encoded in the shape or the pattern of the spikes. Location is coded separately by which part of a map is active, and intensity by firing rate along the same line.

cards.q: How does a single sensory neuron code the intensity of a stimulus?
cards.a: By its firing frequency.
options: By the height of its action potentials
By the conduction velocity of its axon
By the duration of each action potential
By its firing frequency
cards.explanation: Stronger stimuli make a larger receptor potential, the trigger zone returns to threshold sooner, and spikes come faster, so intensity lives in spikes per second. Spike height and duration are fixed by the all or none properties of the membrane, and conduction velocity is set by axon diameter and myelination, all of which stay constant while intensity changes.

cards.q: Besides firing frequency, what is the second way the nervous system codes a stronger stimulus?
cards.a: More receptors are recruited, so more afferent fibers are active.
options: The action potentials grow larger in the strongest fibers
The stimulus is switched onto a faster conducting pathway instead
More receptors are recruited, so more afferent fibers are active
The refractory period shortens so spikes can overlap
cards.explanation: A stronger stimulus spreads farther and reaches receptors with higher thresholds, so the population of active afferents grows, and this population code works alongside frequency coding. Spike amplitude never changes with intensity, pathways are fixed rather than switched by strength, and the refractory period is a property of the channels and does not shorten with a bigger stimulus.

cards.q: How is the location of a touch stimulus coded?
cards.a: By which receptors are active and where their pathway ends in the cortical map.
options: By which receptors are active and where their pathway ends in the cortical map
By the firing frequency of the activated afferent fibers
By the conduction velocity of the afferent fibers that carry the signal upward
By the interval between the onset and the offset of firing
cards.explanation: Each afferent monitors one small patch of skin, and its central endings land at a fixed spot in the somatosensory map, so activity at a given spot in the map means a stimulus at the matching spot on the body. Frequency carries intensity instead, conduction velocity mostly reflects fiber type and modality, and the timing of onset and offset carries duration.

cards.q: How is the duration of a stimulus coded in a slowly adapting receptor?
cards.a: By how long the train of action potentials continues.
options: By the total number of afferent fibers recruited
By the size of the first action potential in the train
By the conduction velocity of the afferent fiber
By how long the train of action potentials continues
cards.explanation: A tonic receptor keeps firing for as long as the stimulus is applied, so the length of the train maps onto the length of the stimulus. The number of fibers recruited codes intensity, spike size is fixed, and conduction velocity does not vary with how long a stimulus is held. Rapidly adapting receptors give up this duration information, which is the tradeoff for reporting change sharply.

cards.q: A blow to the eye makes a person see a flash of light rather than feel a thud. Which principle does this illustrate?
cards.a: The law of specific nerve energies, a form of the labeled line principle.
options: Frequency coding of stimulus intensity in the afferent fiber
The law of specific nerve energies, a form of the labeled line principle
Population coding through the recruitment of additional receptors
Lateral inhibition sharpening the border between stimulated and unstimulated skin
cards.explanation: However you activate a sensory line, the brain interprets the traffic as the modality that line is labeled for, so mechanically activating the visual pathway produces light. Frequency and population coding both concern intensity, not modality, and lateral inhibition sharpens location. This principle is the reason a single afferent cannot be repurposed to carry a different sensation.

cards.q: Coding stimulus intensity as the number of action potentials per second is called what?
cards.a: Frequency coding.
options: Population coding
Labeled line coding
Frequency coding
Temporal summation
cards.explanation: Frequency coding is the rate based signal carried by a single afferent, and it is the primary intensity code. Population coding is the parallel signal carried by how many afferents are recruited, and labeled line coding carries modality rather than intensity. Temporal summation is a mechanism at the membrane that helps build the receptor potential, not a code the brain reads.

cards.q: A finger presses on the skin, then presses twice as hard. What happens to the population code?
cards.a: Active afferents fire faster and higher threshold afferents are recruited.
options: Active afferents fire faster while the number of active afferents falls off
Active afferents fire faster and higher threshold afferents are recruited
The same afferents fire at the same rate but switch to a different pathway
Fewer afferents fire, but each one fires a larger action potential
cards.explanation: Both intensity codes move together: existing afferents raise their rate and the stronger stimulus spreads far enough to cross the threshold of receptors that were silent before. A stronger stimulus never reduces the number of active fibers, modality pathways are fixed and are not swapped by intensity, and spike amplitude is constant. The brain uses the two signals together to judge how hard the press was.

cards.q: A cochlear implant delivers electrical pulses directly to the auditory nerve, bypassing the hair cells. Why does the patient hear sound rather than feel a shock?
cards.a: The auditory nerve is a labeled line, so any activity on it is read as sound.
options: The pulses are shaped to look like the receptor potentials of hair cells
The electrical current is too weak to activate any pain fibers
The auditory nerve is a labeled line, so any activity on it is read as sound
The cortex learns over time to relabel the pulses as sound
cards.explanation: Modality is set by where the pathway terminates centrally, so activity arriving on the auditory nerve is interpreted as sound no matter what started it, which is exactly what makes the implant possible. The shape of the stimulus does not carry modality, since all action potentials look alike. The current strength and the patient's experience over time affect quality and clarity, not the basic category of the sensation.

cards.q: A touch moves from the index fingertip to the palm. How does the CNS register that the location changed, given that the modality is the same?
cards.a: A different set of afferents fires, reaching a different point in the cortical map.
options: A different set of afferents fires, reaching a different point in the cortical map
The same afferents change their firing frequency to signal the new site
The signal switches from the dorsal column pathway to the spinothalamic pathway instead
The conduction velocity changes because the palm is closer to the cord
cards.explanation: Location is a spatial code: each afferent covers one patch of skin and projects to a fixed point in the somatosensory map, so moving the stimulus lights up a different point on that map. Frequency codes intensity rather than place, and pathway choice codes modality, which has not changed here. Small differences in conduction distance are not used as a location signal.

cards.q: A steady pressure is held on the skin for 10 seconds instead of 1 second. In a tonic receptor, what does the recording show?
cards.a: A train of action potentials that lasts about ten times longer.
options: A train ten times faster but of the same total length
A single burst that is ten times larger in amplitude
Two bursts, one at onset and one at offset, separated by silence
A train of action potentials that lasts about ten times longer
cards.explanation: Tonic receptors adapt slowly, so they keep firing for as long as the stimulus is present and the length of the train is the duration signal. Firing rate would only change if the pressure changed, spike amplitude is fixed, and the on and off burst pattern with silence in between is the signature of a rapidly adapting phasic receptor, which reports change and not duration.

cards.q: Perceived intensity grows roughly with the logarithm of stimulus strength. Which added weight is easier to notice, 10 g added to a 20 g object or 10 g added to a 500 g object?
cards.a: The 10 g added to the 20 g object.
options: Both are equally noticeable, since the added weight is the same
The 10 g added to the 20 g object
The 10 g added to the 500 g object
Neither can be noticed, since 10 g is below threshold
cards.explanation: A logarithmic relationship means the system responds to proportional change, so 10 g on 20 g is a 50 percent increase and easy to detect while 10 g on 500 g is a 2 percent increase and easy to miss. The absolute size of the added weight is not what the receptors report. This compression is what lets one afferent cover an enormous range of stimulus strengths with a limited firing rate.

cards.q: As a pinprick becomes progressively sharper, receptors that were silent begin to fire. What is this called?
cards.a: Recruitment, the basis of population coding.
options: Recruitment, the basis of population coding
Adaptation, the decline of firing during a steady stimulus
Lateral inhibition, the sharpening of a stimulus border
Convergence, the pooling of afferents onto one central neuron
cards.explanation: Receptors differ in threshold, so raising intensity brings the higher threshold ones above their thresholds and the active population grows, which is recruitment. Adaptation runs the other way, reducing firing during a maintained stimulus. Lateral inhibition sharpens where a stimulus is, and convergence is an anatomical arrangement that blurs location rather than a code for intensity.

cards.q: Why does the brain not need to examine the shape or pattern of arriving action potentials to know whether a signal means cold or pressure?
cards.a: Because modality is already specified by which labeled line the signal arrives on.
options: Because cold and pressure spikes differ in amplitude by the time they reach cortex
Because the thalamus rewrites the spike pattern before it reaches the cortex
Because cold signals arrive faster and can be sorted by arrival time
Because modality is already specified by which labeled line the signal arrives on
cards.explanation: Every action potential in the body looks essentially the same, so modality has to be carried by anatomy rather than by waveform, and the terminating site in cortex supplies that information. Spike amplitude does not vary by modality, the thalamus relays and gates rather than recoding modality, and although fiber types do differ in speed, arrival time is not a reliable modality code.

cards.q: A recording from one afferent shows a burst of spikes when a weight is placed on the skin, silence while the weight sits there, and a second burst when the weight is lifted. What does this afferent code well, and what does it code poorly?
cards.a: It codes onset and offset well but codes duration poorly.
options: It codes duration well but codes stimulus intensity poorly
It codes location well but codes modality poorly
It codes onset and offset well but codes duration poorly
It codes intensity well but codes onset poorly
cards.explanation: This is a rapidly adapting receptor, and its silence during the maintained stimulus means the CNS has no ongoing report that the weight is still there, so duration information is lost from this line. What the pattern does deliver precisely is when the stimulus started and when it ended. Modality and location are still fully specified by which labeled line is firing, and intensity is still carried in the size of each burst.

cards.q: After an arm amputation, tapping the cut end of the nerve in the stump makes the patient feel a distinct touch in the missing hand. Explain the sensation using stimulus coding.
cards.a: The afferent is a labeled line for the hand, so its activity is referred there.
options: The afferent is a labeled line for the hand, so its activity is referred there
The cortex has already remapped, so it now assigns the sensation to the stump
Tapping produces a stronger stimulus, and stronger stimuli are perceived more distally
The nerve regenerated far enough that the hand receptors are firing again
cards.explanation: Modality and location are both set by which line is active and where it terminates centrally, so a fiber that used to report the hand still reports the hand even when the stimulus is applied to its midpoint. Cortical remapping does occur after amputation, but it does not relabel the stump as the source of these sensations. Intensity does not shift perceived location, and there are no hand receptors left to regenerate to.

cards.q: One afferent fires at 40 spikes per second when a weak stimulus lands at the center of its receptive field, and at the same 40 spikes per second when a strong stimulus lands at the edge. How does the CNS avoid misjudging intensity?
cards.a: By comparing across the population, since a strong stimulus recruits more afferents.
options: By waiting for the afferent to adapt, since only strong stimuli cause adaptation
By comparing across the population, since a strong stimulus recruits more afferents
By measuring the amplitude of the action potentials, which is larger for strong stimuli
By checking the conduction velocity, which rises with stimulus strength
cards.explanation: A single afferent is genuinely ambiguous here, since its firing rate confounds intensity with position in its receptive field, and the population code resolves it because a strong stimulus recruits many neighboring afferents while a weak central one recruits few. Adaptation depends on receptor type rather than on strength, spike amplitude is fixed, and conduction velocity does not vary with stimulus strength. This is a good example of why two intensity codes are better than one.

cards.q: A drug halves the firing rate of every somatosensory afferent in one hand without silencing any of them or changing which fibers are active. Predict the effect on the four coded features.
cards.a: Intensity is underreported, while modality, location, and duration survive.
options: Modality is lost, while intensity, location, and duration are preserved
Location is lost, while modality, intensity, and duration are preserved
All four features are lost, because every one of the codes depends on firing rate
Intensity is underreported, while modality, location, and duration survive
cards.explanation: Firing rate is the intensity code, so halving it makes every stimulus feel weaker than it is. Modality still depends on which labeled lines are active, location still depends on which part of the map they reach, and duration still depends on how long the trains last, and none of those three has been changed. This is exactly why the nervous system spreads the four features across different codes rather than packing them all into rate.

cards.q: What is the receptive field of a sensory neuron?
cards.a: The region of the body where a stimulus changes that neuron's firing.
options: The region of the body where a stimulus changes that neuron's firing
The region of cortex where the signal from that neuron finally arrives
The range of stimulus intensities the neuron can code
The range of modalities the neuron is able to transduce
cards.explanation: A receptive field is a patch of skin, or of retina, and stimulating anywhere in that patch alters the firing of the one neuron that owns it. The cortical destination is a separate idea, the target of the labeled line rather than the field itself. Intensity range and modality are properties of the receptor, not a description of where it listens.

cards.q: What does a two point discrimination test measure?
cards.a: The smallest separation at which two simultaneous touches are felt as two.
options: The smallest force that can be detected anywhere on the skin
The time between two touches needed to feel them as separate
The smallest separation at which two simultaneous touches are felt as two
The number of touch receptors present in a square centimeter of skin
cards.explanation: The examiner sets two points a known distance apart, touches the skin with both at once, and finds the distance at which the subject stops feeling one point and starts feeling two, which is the two point threshold. The smallest detectable force is the touch threshold, a different measurement. Temporal separation and receptor counts are related ideas but neither is what this test reports.

cards.q: How does receptive field size relate to tactile acuity?
cards.a: Smaller receptive fields give finer acuity.
options: Larger receptive fields give finer acuity
Smaller receptive fields give finer acuity
Receptive field size has no effect on acuity
Acuity is best when fields are of medium size
cards.explanation: If each afferent watches a tiny patch of skin, two nearby points are likely to fall in two different fields and activate two different lines, which the brain reads as two points. A large field swallows both points into one line and they are felt as one. This single relationship is what makes fingertips sharp and the back coarse.

cards.q: What is lateral inhibition in a sensory pathway?
cards.a: A strongly stimulated pathway inhibits its neighbors through interneurons.
options: A stimulus inhibits the receptor that transduced it, which ends the response
A pathway inhibits itself after firing, producing the refractory period
Two pathways carrying different modalities inhibit one another in the thalamus
A strongly stimulated pathway inhibits its neighbors through interneurons
cards.explanation: The most active afferent pathway sends collaterals to inhibitory interneurons that suppress the second order neurons on either side, so weakly stimulated neighbors are silenced and the center of the stimulus stands out. Self inhibition after firing is adaptation or refractoriness, and cross modality inhibition is not what this circuit does. Lateral inhibition is what sharpens location beyond what receptor spacing alone would allow.

cards.q: How does receptor density in a patch of skin relate to two point threshold?
cards.a: Higher density gives a smaller two point threshold.
options: Higher density gives a larger two point threshold
Higher density gives a smaller two point threshold
Density affects sensitivity to force but not two point threshold
Density and two point threshold are unrelated
cards.explanation: Packing more afferents into the same area means each one covers less skin, so two nearby points are more likely to stimulate separate afferents and be felt separately, and the threshold distance shrinks. Density and field size are two ways of describing the same anatomy. Density does also affect force sensitivity, but that is an additional effect and not a substitute for this one.

cards.q: Which body region has the finest two point discrimination?
cards.a: The fingertips and lips.
options: The upper back
The anterior thigh
The fingertips and lips
The back of the calf
cards.explanation: The fingertips and lips are packed with small field mechanoreceptors and are the surfaces the body uses to explore fine detail, so their two point thresholds are the smallest on the body. The back, thigh, and calf all have sparse receptors with large overlapping fields and thresholds tens of millimeters wide. Acuity tracks how much detail a region needs to resolve, not how much surface area it has.

cards.q: Which body region has the coarsest two point discrimination?
cards.a: The middle of the back.
options: The middle of the back
The palm of the hand
The tip of the tongue
The side of the nose
cards.explanation: The back has the largest receptive fields and the lowest receptor density of the sites listed, so two points must be separated by several centimeters before they feel like two. The palm is intermediate, and the tongue tip and nose are both high acuity surfaces used for fine discrimination. The pattern to remember is that surfaces used for exploration are sharp and surfaces used mainly for protection are coarse.

cards.q: Roughly what two point threshold would you expect at the fingertip in a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 2 to 3 mm.
options: About 0.05 mm
About 20 to 30 mm
About 60 to 70 mm
About 2 to 3 mm
cards.explanation: Fingertip thresholds sit around 2 to 3 mm, which is why fingertips can read raised dots and judge fine texture. A value near 0.05 mm is finer than the spacing of the receptors themselves and is not achievable. Values in the 20 to 30 mm range fit the forearm or upper arm, and 60 to 70 mm fits the back or calf.

cards.q: Two calipers touch the forearm 15 mm apart and the subject reports feeling a single point. What does that tell you about the receptive fields there?
cards.a: Both points fell within the receptive field of one afferent population.
options: The receptive fields there are smaller than 15 mm across
Both points fell within the receptive field of one afferent population
Lateral inhibition failed, so the two separate signals merged into one
The subject's touch threshold for force is elevated
cards.explanation: Feeling one point means the nervous system had only one active line to report, which happens when both caliper tips land inside one large receptive field. Fields smaller than the separation would have produced two separate signals and the report of two points. Lateral inhibition would sharpen the perception rather than merge it, and detecting the touch at all shows the force threshold is fine.

cards.q: A pencil eraser is pressed on the skin. Lateral inhibition in the pathway makes the perceived edge of the contact sharper. How does it do that?
cards.a: It suppresses the weakly stimulated pathways just outside the contact area.
options: It suppresses the weakly stimulated pathways just outside the contact area
It raises the firing rate of every pathway inside the contact area
It slows conduction in the neighboring pathways so their signals arrive late
It shrinks the receptive fields of the afferents under the eraser
cards.explanation: Afferents at the edge of the contact are stimulated less than those at the center, and inhibition from the strongly firing center silences them, so the contrast between the active center and the quiet surround becomes sharp. Nothing in the circuit boosts the center, though the relative difference makes it seem that way. Conduction speed is unchanged, and receptive field size is anatomical and does not shrink from moment to moment.

cards.q: You measure two point thresholds at the index fingertip and at the upper arm in the same subject. Which result should you predict?
cards.a: The fingertip threshold is much smaller than the upper arm threshold.
options: The two thresholds are about equal, since both are skin
The upper arm threshold is much smaller than the fingertip threshold
The fingertip threshold is smaller only if the fingertip is warmed first
The fingertip threshold is much smaller than the upper arm threshold
cards.explanation: The fingertip has dense receptors with small fields and the upper arm has sparse receptors with large fields, so the fingertip separates two points at a few millimeters while the upper arm needs several centimeters. Skin is not uniform, so equal thresholds should never be expected. Temperature can shift sensitivity somewhat, but the difference between these sites is anatomical and holds without any warming.

cards.q: In a region of skin, twenty afferents converge onto a single second order neuron in the spinal cord. What is the effect on acuity there?
cards.a: Acuity is poor, because the second order neuron has a large receptive field.
options: Acuity is sharp, because twenty afferents give twenty times the detail
Acuity is unchanged, since acuity is set at the receptor only
Acuity is poor, because the second order neuron has a large receptive field
Acuity is sharp, because convergence produces stronger lateral inhibition
cards.explanation: Convergence means the second order neuron fires no matter which of the twenty afferents was stimulated, so it reports a large area rather than a point and detail is thrown away at that synapse. More afferents feeding one cell adds sensitivity, not resolution. High acuity regions do the opposite, keeping convergence low so each central neuron still speaks for a tiny patch of skin.

cards.q: A drug blocks the inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal column nuclei. What happens to the localization of a point touch?
cards.a: It becomes blurred, because activity spreads to neighboring pathways.
options: It becomes sharper, because more pathways are now active
It becomes blurred, because activity spreads to neighboring pathways
It is unchanged, because localization is determined entirely at the receptor
It is lost completely, because the touch no longer reaches cortex
cards.explanation: Lateral inhibition is what silences the weakly stimulated surround, so removing it leaves a broad hill of activity instead of a sharp peak, and the subject can feel the touch but not place it precisely. More active pathways means less contrast, not more. Receptor anatomy sets a limit on acuity, but central inhibition sharpens within that limit, and the excitatory pathway to cortex is untouched.

cards.q: A single afferent is recorded while a fine probe is moved across the skin. Firing increases at several nearby spots and stops beyond them. What have you mapped?
cards.a: The receptive field of that afferent.
options: The receptive field of that afferent
The two point threshold at that site
The lateral inhibition zone of that afferent
The cortical representation of that skin area
cards.explanation: The set of skin positions where the probe changes that one neuron's firing is the definition of its receptive field, and the boundary is where the firing stops. A two point threshold requires two simultaneous stimuli and a subject's report, not a single probe and a recording. The inhibitory surround would show as decreased firing, and cortical representation is measured centrally rather than on the skin.

cards.q: Braille is read with the fingertips rather than the palm or the forearm. Which physiological fact explains the choice?
cards.a: Fingertip receptive fields are small enough to resolve dots 2 mm apart.
options: Fingertip skin is thinner, so the stimuli reach the receptors more quickly
Fingertip receptors adapt more slowly, so the dots are felt for longer
Fingertip afferents conduct faster, so the whole pattern arrives sooner
Fingertip receptive fields are small enough to resolve dots 2 mm apart
cards.explanation: Braille dots sit two to three millimeters apart, which is right at the fingertip two point threshold and far below the threshold of the palm or forearm, so only the fingertip can report them as separate. Skin thickness and conduction speed affect timing rather than spatial resolution. Fingertip mechanoreceptors are in fact largely rapidly adapting, which suits scanning movement, so slow adaptation is not the reason either.

cards.q: Months after a nerve injury, an area of skin is reinnervated but by fewer afferents than before, so each surviving afferent now serves a much larger patch. Predict the two point threshold there.
cards.a: It is larger than normal, because larger fields merge nearby points.
options: It is smaller than normal, because the surviving afferents are more sensitive
It is unchanged, because two point discrimination depends only on cortex
It is larger than normal, because larger fields merge nearby points
It is unmeasurable, because reinnervated skin cannot feel touch
cards.explanation: Two point threshold tracks receptive field size directly, so when each afferent covers more skin, two points must be moved farther apart before they fall on separate lines and are felt as two. Extra sensitivity to force does not buy spatial resolution, and cortex cannot recover detail the periphery never sent. The skin does feel touch, which is exactly why the threshold can be measured and found to be coarse.

cards.q: A point stimulus strongly excites the second order neuron at the center of the stimulated zone and weakly excites the two neighbors on either side. After lateral inhibition acts, what does the output pattern look like?
cards.a: A strong center with the neighbors silenced, giving a sharp peak.
options: All three neurons firing at the same moderate rate
A strong center with the neighbors silenced, giving a sharp peak
The neighbors firing strongly and the center silenced
All three neurons are silenced, since the inhibition exceeds the excitation
cards.explanation: The most excited neuron sends the most drive into the inhibitory interneurons, so it suppresses its weakly excited neighbors far more than they suppress it, and the result is a narrow peak of activity where a broad hill would otherwise be. Equal firing across all three is exactly the blurred pattern the circuit exists to prevent. The center wins rather than loses this competition, and total silencing would erase the stimulus.

cards.q: Site A has a two point threshold of 3 mm and site B has one of 45 mm. What can you infer about receptive field size and cortical territory at the two sites?
cards.a: Site A has smaller fields and a larger cortical territory per unit of skin than site B.
options: Site A has smaller fields and a larger cortical territory per unit of skin than site B
Site A has smaller fields and a smaller cortical territory per unit of skin than site B
Site A has larger fields and a larger cortical territory per unit of skin than site B
The thresholds tell you about fields but say nothing about cortical territory
cards.explanation: A small threshold means small, densely packed receptive fields, and keeping those separate lines separate all the way up requires many central neurons, so high acuity skin claims a disproportionately large slice of somatosensory cortex. Small fields with little cortex would waste the peripheral detail, and large fields cannot produce a 3 mm threshold. The three measures, threshold, field size, and cortical area, move together in a predictable way.

cards.q: A recording across a row of second order neurons shows a broad, flat hill of firing after a point touch, where a sharp peak is normally seen. The afferents themselves respond normally. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a: Lateral inhibition in the pathway has been lost.
options: The receptors have adapted and stopped firing
The stimulus was applied for too short a time to be coded
The afferent receptive fields have shrunk
Lateral inhibition in the pathway has been lost
cards.explanation: Normal afferent responses place the problem central to the receptors, and the specific loss of contrast between the peak and its surround is the signature of a missing inhibitory surround. Adaptation would reduce firing everywhere rather than broaden it, and too brief a stimulus would produce less activity, not a wider hill. Shrinking the receptive fields would sharpen the profile, which is the opposite of what is recorded.

cards.q: What does receptor adaptation mean?
cards.a: A decline in firing rate during a stimulus that is held constant.
options: A rise in firing rate as a stimulus is held constant
A decline in firing rate during a stimulus that is held constant
A change in the modality a receptor reports over time
A shift of the receptor's response to a different body region
cards.explanation: Adaptation is the fall in action potential frequency that occurs while the stimulus itself stays the same, so the receptor stops reporting a condition it has already reported. Firing that increases during a steady stimulus is sensitization, which happens at nociceptors during inflammation. Modality is fixed by the labeled line, and receptive field position is anatomical, so neither drifts with time.

cards.q: How does a tonic receptor behave during a maintained stimulus?
cards.a: It adapts slowly and fires for as long as the stimulus lasts.
options: It fires once at onset and then falls silent
It fires only when the stimulus is removed
It adapts within a few milliseconds and then stops firing entirely
It adapts slowly and fires for as long as the stimulus lasts
cards.explanation: Tonic receptors are the slowly adapting group, and their sustained firing is what lets the CNS know a condition is still present, though the rate may drift down somewhat. Firing only at onset, only at offset, or for a few milliseconds all describe phasic receptors. The distinction between the two groups is the rate of adaptation, not the strength of the response.

cards.q: How does a phasic receptor behave during a maintained stimulus?
cards.a: It fires at the onset, adapts quickly, and often fires again at the offset.
options: It fires at the onset, adapts quickly, and often fires again at the offset
It fires steadily from onset until the stimulus is removed
It fires with slowly increasing frequency the longer the stimulus lasts
It fires only if the stimulus lasts longer than one second
cards.explanation: Phasic receptors are rapidly adapting and are built to report change, so they signal that something started and that something stopped and stay quiet in between. Steady firing throughout is the tonic pattern. Firing that grows over time would be sensitization, and phasic receptors respond best to brief and changing stimuli rather than requiring long ones.

cards.q: Which of these is a slowly adapting, tonic receptor?
cards.a: The muscle spindle.
options: The Pacinian corpuscle
The Meissner corpuscle
The muscle spindle
The olfactory receptor
cards.explanation: The muscle spindle reports muscle length continuously, which posture requires, so it must adapt slowly. Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles are both rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors tuned to vibration and to moving light touch, and olfactory receptors adapt so quickly that a smell fades within minutes. The match is always between how long the body needs the information and how slowly the receptor adapts.

cards.q: Which of these is a rapidly adapting, phasic receptor?
cards.a: The Pacinian corpuscle.
options: The Merkel disc
The Pacinian corpuscle
The nociceptor
The carotid sinus baroreceptor
cards.explanation: The Pacinian corpuscle has onion like lamellae that slip and redistribute a steady pressure away from the ending, so it responds only to changing pressure and is the classic vibration detector. Merkel discs report sustained pressure and texture, nociceptors adapt very little, and baroreceptors fire continuously at normal arterial pressures, so all three are slowly adapting.

cards.q: Which receptor type produces a burst of firing at both the onset and the offset of a stimulus?
cards.a: A phasic receptor.
options: A tonic receptor
A nociceptive receptor
A chemoreceptor
A phasic receptor
cards.explanation: On and off responses come from a receptor that reports change and ignores steady state, which is the definition of the rapidly adapting, phasic group. A tonic receptor fills in the middle of that pattern with continuous firing. Nociceptor and chemoreceptor name the stimulus class rather than the adaptation rate, and receptors in either class can in principle adapt fast or slowly.

cards.q: Which type of receptor is best suited to reporting joint position continuously while a person stands still?
cards.a: A tonic receptor.
options: A tonic receptor
A phasic receptor
A rapidly adapting receptor
A receptor with an on and off response
cards.explanation: Standing still requires a signal that is present the whole time, and only a slowly adapting, tonic receptor keeps sending one. The other three options all name the same rapidly adapting group in different words, and that group would report the moment the joint moved and then go quiet, leaving posture unmonitored. Matching adaptation rate to how long the information is needed is the core skill in this competency.

cards.q: Nociceptors adapt very little, and some sensitize instead. Why is that useful?
cards.a: Tissue damage keeps mattering, so the warning must not fade away.
options: It allows pain to be located more precisely than touch
It keeps the pain fibers from conducting too quickly
Tissue damage keeps mattering, so the warning must not fade away
It prevents nociceptors from responding to more than one type of stimulus
cards.explanation: Adaptation is useful when a signal has already done its job, and a damaging stimulus never has, so a nociceptor that faded would let a person keep a hand on a hot pan. Pain is in fact localized less precisely than touch, not more. Adaptation rate has no bearing on conduction velocity, and many nociceptors are polymodal, responding to several stimulus types.

cards.q: You stop noticing the feeling of your shirt a minute after putting it on, though the shirt is still there. Which receptors explain this?
cards.a: Phasic mechanoreceptors, which adapted to the steady pressure.
options: Phasic mechanoreceptors, which adapted to the steady pressure
Tonic mechanoreceptors, which continue to fire but are ignored
Nociceptors, which adapted once the pressure proved harmless
Thermoreceptors, which stopped reporting the warmth of the fabric
cards.explanation: The rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors of the skin fire as the shirt settles and then fall silent, so the CNS receives no ongoing touch signal at all, which is why moving the shirt makes you notice it again at once. Tonic receptors do keep some steady traffic going, but the disappearance of the sensation reflects adaptation in the periphery rather than a decision to ignore it. Nociceptors are not activated by a shirt, and the thermal signal is a separate sensation from the touch that fades.

cards.q: In an experiment the lamellae are peeled away from a Pacinian corpuscle, leaving the bare nerve ending. Steady pressure is then applied. What is the predicted result?
cards.a: The ending fires throughout the pressure rather than only at its onset.
options: The ending stops responding to any applied pressure at all
The ending fires only at the offset of the applied pressure
The ending fires action potentials of much larger amplitude than before
The ending fires throughout the pressure rather than only at its onset
cards.explanation: The lamellae are what make the corpuscle phasic, because they slip under maintained pressure and stop transmitting force to the ending, so removing them leaves an ending that stays deformed and keeps firing. This is the cleanest demonstration that adaptation can be built into accessory structures rather than into the membrane. Transduction still works, so the response is not abolished, and spike height is fixed by the all or none rule.

cards.q: Arterial pressure must be monitored beat after beat, all day. What does that require of the carotid sinus baroreceptors?
cards.a: They must adapt slowly enough to keep firing at a steady mean pressure.
options: They must adapt within a second so each beat is reported separately
They must adapt slowly enough to keep firing at a steady mean pressure
They must stop firing between beats to avoid saturating the pathway
They must switch from tonic to phasic behavior once pressure is stable
cards.explanation: A control system that corrects blood pressure needs a continuous readout of the current pressure, so the sensor has to keep reporting rather than falling silent, which is tonic behavior. A sensor that adapted in a second would leave the medulla blind between beats. Baroreceptors do reset over days if pressure stays high, but that is slow drift, not the moment to moment silence a phasic receptor would show.

cards.q: A person walks into a kitchen, notices a strong smell, and within a few minutes cannot detect it, though the odor molecules are still in the air. What accounts for this?
cards.a: Olfactory receptors adapt rapidly to a constant odor concentration.
options: The odor molecules are cleared from the nasal mucosa within minutes
The olfactory nerve fatigues and can no longer conduct action potentials
Olfactory receptors adapt rapidly to a constant odor concentration
The cortex switches the labeled line for that odor to another modality
cards.explanation: Olfactory receptors are strongly phasic, so a steady concentration produces a burst of firing and then near silence, which is why a new smell in the same room is still detected while the old one is not. The molecules are still arriving, so clearance is not the explanation. Axons do not fatigue in this way over minutes, and labeled lines are fixed anatomy that the cortex cannot reassign.

cards.q: Two afferents are recorded during a five second skin indentation. Afferent A fires briskly for the whole five seconds. Afferent B fires for 100 ms at the start and 100 ms at the end. Which is which?
cards.a: A is tonic and B is phasic.
options: A is tonic and B is phasic
A is phasic and B is tonic
Both are tonic, but B has a higher threshold
Both are phasic, but A has a larger receptive field
cards.explanation: Continuous firing throughout the stimulus is the definition of slow adaptation, and brief bursts confined to onset and offset are the definition of rapid adaptation, so the recordings identify the two types directly. Threshold and receptive field size are separate properties that would change how easily and where each afferent responds, not how its firing decays over time. Reading the two patterns off a tracing is the practical form of this distinction.

cards.q: Why would it be a poor design for the receptors that detect a light touch on the arm to adapt as slowly as nociceptors do?
cards.a: The CNS would be flooded with signals about unchanging contact.
options: Touch receptors would then be unable to code the intensity of a stimulus
The touch pathway would be too slow to reach cortex in time
Touch receptors would begin to report pain instead of pressure
The CNS would be flooded with signals about unchanging contact
cards.explanation: Adaptation is a filter that keeps the nervous system focused on new and changing information, and a steady, harmless contact carries no news after the first moment. Intensity coding by firing rate works in both tonic and phasic receptors, so it would not be lost. Conduction speed is unrelated to adaptation, and modality is fixed by the labeled line, so a touch receptor cannot start signaling pain.

cards.q: A vibrating tuning fork is placed against the skin. Which adaptation property makes a receptor good at detecting the vibration?
cards.a: Rapid adaptation, so it can respond to each cycle of pressure change.
options: Slow adaptation, so it can report the total time the fork is applied for
Rapid adaptation, so it can respond to each cycle of pressure change
Slow adaptation, so it can report the amplitude of each cycle
No adaptation at all, so no information is ever discarded
cards.explanation: Vibration is a rapid series of pressure changes, and only a receptor that resets quickly between them can fire in step with each cycle rather than blurring them together. A slowly adapting receptor stays partly depolarized from the previous cycle and loses the timing information. Reporting total application time or refusing to adapt at all would preserve less useful information, not more, for a stimulus whose content is the change itself.

cards.q: A patient has had untreated hypertension for years. Over that time the carotid sinus baroreceptors have reset to the higher pressure. What does the reflex now defend, and what does that mean for treatment?
cards.a: It defends the new higher pressure, so lowering pressure triggers compensation.
options: It defends normal pressure, so the reflex opposes the hypertension continuously
It defends the new higher pressure, so lowering pressure triggers compensation
It defends nothing, because reset baroreceptors stop firing altogether
It defends only pulse pressure, since mean pressure is no longer sensed
cards.explanation: Resetting is adaptation on a slow time scale: the receptors come to treat the chronically high pressure as their new baseline, so they fire normally there and respond to changes around it. That is why a drug that lowers pressure is read as a fall and is met with reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction until the receptors reset again. If the reflex still defended the original normal, chronic hypertension would be self correcting, and reset receptors are still firing rather than silent.

cards.q: A drug converts the rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors of the skin into slowly adapting ones without changing anything else. Predict the effect on everyday sensation.
cards.a: Steady contact would be felt continuously, and vibration would be felt poorly.
options: Steady contact would be felt continuously, and vibration would be felt poorly
Steady contact would still fade away, but vibration would be felt more sharply
Pain would be felt continuously and touch would disappear
Nothing would change, since perception is decided in the cortex
cards.explanation: Slow adaptation means the ending keeps reporting a constant pressure, so the shirt never stops being felt, and it also means the receptor cannot reset fast enough to follow each cycle of a vibration, so high frequency detection suffers. Fading contact requires the rapid adaptation the drug removed. Nociceptors are a separate population and are unaffected, and cortex can only work with the traffic the periphery sends.

cards.q: A recording during a ramp and hold indentation shows a high firing rate while the probe is moving in, a lower but steady rate while the probe is held, and a brief pause when the probe withdraws. How should this afferent be described?
cards.a: Slowly adapting, with an added sensitivity to the rate of change.
options: Rapidly adapting, since the firing rate falls after the ramp
Slowly adapting, with an added sensitivity to the rate of change
Rapidly adapting, since firing stops when the probe withdraws
Non adapting, since firing never falls to zero during the hold
cards.explanation: The maintained firing during the hold is the defining feature and marks the afferent as slowly adapting, while the higher rate during the ramp shows it also reports how fast the skin is being indented, a dynamic component many tonic receptors have. A drop in rate after the ramp is not the same as adapting to silence, which is what rapidly adapting means. Firing that continues at a lower level is still adaptation, so calling it non adapting overstates the case.
