cards.q: Imagine a hand in which every mechanoreceptor is phasic and none are tonic. Which everyday task becomes hardest?
cards.a: Holding a glass with steady grip force without watching it.
options: Feeling a fly land on the skin
Detecting the buzz of a phone in the palm
Noticing the exact moment a held object begins to slip in the hand
Holding a glass with steady grip force without watching it
cards.explanation: Grip force control depends on a continuous report of how hard the fingers are pressing, and with only rapidly adapting receptors that report vanishes a moment after the grasp is stable, so the glass is squeezed or dropped without visual feedback. The other three tasks are all detections of change, which is precisely what phasic receptors do best. This is the clearest demonstration of why the body keeps both types rather than choosing one.

cards.q: Where is the cell body of the first order neuron of a somatosensory pathway?
cards.a: In the dorsal root ganglion.
options: In the dorsal horn of the spinal cord
In the dorsal root ganglion
In the ventral posterior nucleus of the thalamus
In the postcentral gyrus of the cortex
cards.explanation: The first order neuron runs from the receptor to the CNS with its cell body parked in the dorsal root ganglion, off to the side of the conducting axon. The dorsal horn is where many first order neurons synapse onto second order neurons, not where their cell bodies sit. The thalamus holds third order cell bodies, and the postcentral gyrus is the final destination rather than a cell body location for the pathway neurons.

cards.q: Which sensations travel in the dorsal column medial lemniscus pathway?
cards.a: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception.
options: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception
Pain, temperature, and crude touch
Pain and vibration only
Temperature and conscious proprioception but nothing else
cards.explanation: The dorsal columns carry the large fiber, high acuity information: two point discrimination, vibration, and joint position. Pain, temperature, and crude touch travel instead in the spinothalamic pathway on small diameter fibers. Keeping the two lists separate is what makes it possible to predict which sensations a given cord lesion will take.

cards.q: Where does the dorsal column pathway cross to the opposite side?
cards.a: In the medulla, after the second order neuron begins.
options: At the level of the spinal cord where the fiber enters
In the midbrain, just below the thalamus
In the medulla, after the second order neuron begins
It does not cross at all
cards.explanation: First order fibers ascend the cord on the same side, synapse in the gracile or cuneate nucleus of the medulla, and the second order axon then crosses as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. Crossing near the level of entry is the spinothalamic arrangement, which is why the two pathways behave so differently after a cord lesion. Every conscious somatosensory pathway crosses at some point, since each hemisphere serves the opposite side of the body.

cards.q: Where does the spinothalamic pathway cross to the opposite side?
cards.a: In the spinal cord, within a segment or two of where it enters.
options: In the medulla, at the internal arcuate fibers of the lemniscus
In the midbrain, at about the level of the red nucleus
It does not cross at all, so pain is felt on the same side
In the spinal cord, within a segment or two of where it enters
cards.explanation: Pain and temperature fibers synapse in the dorsal horn almost immediately, and the second order axon crosses in the anterior commissure and ascends on the opposite side. Crossing in the medulla is the dorsal column arrangement. Because both pathways cross somewhere, sensation always reaches the opposite hemisphere, but the level of crossing differs, and that difference produces the split findings of a cord hemisection.

cards.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays somatosensory information from the body to the cortex?
cards.a: The ventral posterior lateral nucleus.
options: The medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
The ventral posterior lateral nucleus
The lateral geniculate nucleus
The anterior nucleus
cards.explanation: The ventral posterior lateral nucleus receives both the medial lemniscus and the spinothalamic tract from the body and sends third order axons to the postcentral gyrus. The medial geniculate is the auditory relay and the lateral geniculate the visual relay, both sensory but for other modalities. The anterior nucleus belongs to limbic circuitry rather than to a sensory relay.

cards.q: Where does the somatosensory pathway terminate in the cortex?
cards.a: In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe.
options: In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
In the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
In the superior temporal gyrus
In the calcarine cortex of the occipital lobe
cards.explanation: Primary somatosensory cortex sits in the postcentral gyrus, immediately behind the central sulcus. The precentral gyrus just in front of that sulcus is primary motor cortex, and confusing the two reverses sensory and motor findings. The superior temporal gyrus is auditory cortex and the calcarine cortex is visual cortex.

cards.q: How many neurons in series carry a touch signal from the skin to the cortex?
cards.a: Three.
options: One
Two
Four
Three
cards.explanation: The chain is first order from receptor to the CNS relay nucleus, second order from that nucleus to the thalamus, and third order from the thalamus to the cortex. A single neuron cannot span the distance and would give no place for the crossing and gating that occur at each synapse. Two would leave out the thalamic relay, which every conscious sensory pathway except olfaction passes through.

cards.q: What determines how much cortical territory a body region receives in the somatosensory homunculus?
cards.a: The density of receptors in that region.
options: The surface area of that region
The muscle mass of that region
The density of receptors in that region
The distance of that region from the brain
cards.explanation: Cortex is allocated by how much information a region sends, and that is set by receptor density, so densely innervated skin such as the fingertips and lips claims a huge strip while broad, sparsely innervated skin such as the back claims very little. Surface area and muscle mass do not predict representation, which is exactly why the map looks distorted. Distance from the brain has no bearing on cortical territory.

cards.q: A pin is felt in the right hand. Which hemisphere processes it, and why?
cards.a: The left hemisphere, because the pathway crossed in the spinal cord.
options: The left hemisphere, because the pathway crossed in the spinal cord
The right hemisphere, because pain pathways stay on the same side
The left hemisphere, because pain pathways cross in the thalamus
Both hemispheres equally, because pain is not localized to one side
cards.explanation: Pain from the right hand enters the right dorsal horn, the second order axon crosses within a segment or two, and the spinothalamic tract ascends on the left to the left thalamus and left cortex. Pain pathways do cross, so a same side answer is wrong, and the crossing happens in the cord rather than in the thalamus, which relays without crossing. Pain localization is imprecise, but it is still lateralized.

cards.q: The left dorsal column is damaged at the C5 level. Which deficit should you predict?
cards.a: Loss of vibration and fine touch in the left arm.
options: Loss of pain and temperature in the left arm
Loss of vibration and fine touch in the left arm
Loss of vibration and fine touch in the right arm
Loss of all sensation in both arms
cards.explanation: Dorsal column fibers ascend on the same side until they reach the medulla, so a lesion below that crossing point causes a deficit on the same side as the damage and below the level of the injury. Pain and temperature are spared because they have already crossed and are travelling in the spinothalamic tract on the other side. A contralateral deficit would require the lesion to be above the medullary crossing.

cards.q: The lips occupy a far larger strip of somatosensory cortex than the entire back. What does that reflect?
cards.a: The lips send far more afferent fibers per square centimeter.
options: The lips move more often than the back
The lips are closer to the brain than the back
The lips contain more muscle tissue per gram than the back does
The lips send far more afferent fibers per square centimeter
cards.explanation: Cortical territory scales with the number of incoming lines, and densely innervated skin with small receptive fields needs many cortical neurons to keep those lines separate. Movement frequency belongs to the motor homunculus rather than the sensory one, distance to the brain is irrelevant to allocation, and muscle mass predicts neither map. This is the same anatomy that gives the lips a two point threshold of a few millimeters.

cards.q: Put these structures in the order a vibration signal from the foot passes through them: medial lemniscus, gracile nucleus, postcentral gyrus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus.
cards.a: Gracile nucleus, medial lemniscus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, postcentral gyrus.
options: Medial lemniscus, gracile nucleus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, postcentral gyrus
Gracile nucleus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, medial lemniscus, postcentral gyrus
Gracile nucleus, medial lemniscus, ventral posterior lateral nucleus, postcentral gyrus
Ventral posterior lateral nucleus, gracile nucleus, medial lemniscus, postcentral gyrus
cards.explanation: The first order fiber ascends the dorsal column and synapses in the gracile nucleus in the medulla, the second order axon crosses and becomes the medial lemniscus, that tract ends in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus, and the third order axon reaches the postcentral gyrus. Placing the medial lemniscus first ignores that the tract is made of second order axons. Putting the thalamus before the lemniscus or at the very start reverses the relay order.

cards.q: Pain fibers synapse in the dorsal horn as soon as they enter the cord, while fine touch fibers ascend for many segments first. What follows from that difference?
cards.a: A cord lesion causes contralateral pain loss but ipsilateral touch loss.
options: A cord lesion causes contralateral pain loss but ipsilateral touch loss
A cord lesion causes ipsilateral loss of both pain and touch below the level
A cord lesion causes contralateral loss of both pain and touch below the level
A cord lesion spares pain entirely, since it has already been relayed
cards.explanation: Because pain crosses at the level of entry, the fibers ascending on one side carry pain from the other side of the body, so damaging them takes pain from the opposite side. Touch fibers have not yet crossed, so damaging them takes touch from the same side. The split pattern is the whole diagnostic value of knowing where each pathway crosses, and relaying in the dorsal horn does not protect the pathway from a lesion higher up.

cards.q: Compare the cortical representation of the hand with that of the trunk. Which is larger, and what does the size predict about acuity?
cards.a: The hand is larger, predicting a much smaller two point threshold there.
options: The trunk is larger, predicting a smaller two point threshold there
The hand is larger, predicting a much smaller two point threshold there
They are equal, since cortical area follows body surface area
The hand is larger, but two point thresholds are the same at both sites
cards.explanation: The hand occupies a disproportionate strip of the postcentral gyrus because it sends dense afferent input with small receptive fields, and that same anatomy produces a fingertip two point threshold of a few millimeters against several centimeters on the trunk. Cortical area follows innervation density rather than surface area, which is why the trunk gets so little despite being large. Cortical territory and acuity move together rather than independently.

cards.q: A patient has a lesion of the right half of the spinal cord at T10. Below that level, what pattern of sensory loss should you predict?
cards.a: Loss of vibration and fine touch on the right leg and loss of pain and temperature on the left leg.
options: Loss of all sensation on the right leg only
Loss of all sensation on the left leg only
Loss of vibration and fine touch on the right leg and loss of pain and temperature on the left leg
Loss of vibration and fine touch on the left leg and loss of pain and temperature on the right leg
cards.explanation: Dorsal column fibers from the right leg are still on the right side at T10, so cutting the right half takes fine touch and vibration from the right leg. Pain and temperature fibers from the left leg crossed near their entry and are ascending on the right, so the same cut takes those modalities from the left leg. Reversing the two sides is the common error, and it comes from forgetting that only one of the two pathways has already crossed at this level.

cards.q: A stroke damages the hand region of the right postcentral gyrus. What should the patient report?
cards.a: Impaired touch and position sense in the left hand, with the right hand normal.
options: Impaired touch and position sense in the right hand, with the left hand normal
Weakness of the right hand with normal sensation
Complete loss of pain sensation in both hands
Impaired touch and position sense in the left hand, with the right hand normal
cards.explanation: Third order axons from the right thalamus serve the right cortex, and the pathway carrying left hand information crossed long before, so a right cortical lesion produces a left sided sensory deficit. Weakness would follow damage to the precentral gyrus one gyrus forward, not to sensory cortex. Bilateral pain loss would require damage on both sides or at a midline structure, and cortical damage rarely abolishes pain awareness entirely.

cards.q: A lesion is found in the left medial lemniscus in the pons. The dorsal columns and the postcentral gyrus are both intact. Which deficit follows?
cards.a: Loss of fine touch and vibration on the right side of the body.
options: Loss of fine touch and vibration on the right side of the body
Loss of fine touch and vibration on the left side of the body
Loss of pain and temperature on the left side of the body
No deficit, since the dorsal columns are intact
cards.explanation: The medial lemniscus is made of second order axons that have already crossed in the medulla, so the left lemniscus carries information from the right side of the body and a lesion there produces a right sided deficit. Intact dorsal columns only mean the signal reaches the medulla, and intact cortex only means the destination can still receive input, so neither rescues a break in the middle of the chain. Pain and temperature travel in the nearby spinothalamic tract and would be spared by a lesion confined to the lemniscus.

cards.q: A violinist has practiced fingering with the left hand for twenty years. Recordings show that the cortical territory devoted to the left fingertips is larger than in a non musician. What does this show about the homunculus?
cards.a: Cortical territory is shaped by input and can change with sustained use.
options: The homunculus is fixed at birth and the recording must be an artifact
Cortical territory is shaped by input and can change with sustained use
Practice increases receptor density, which is the only reason cortex expands
The left hemisphere grows overall, so every body region gains territory
cards.explanation: The map is allocated by input, and heavy, behaviorally important input over years strengthens and expands the cortical territory serving those fingers, which is why trained musicians show enlarged finger representations. A fixed map cannot account for reproducible findings like this one. Receptor density in adult skin does not increase with practice, and the expansion is specific to the trained fingers rather than a general growth of the hemisphere.

cards.q: Which fiber type carries fast pain?
cards.a: Small myelinated A delta fibers.
options: Small myelinated A delta fibers
Unmyelinated C fibers
Large myelinated A beta fibers
Preganglionic autonomic B fibers
cards.explanation: A delta fibers are thin but myelinated, so they conduct at roughly 5 to 30 m/s and deliver the first, sharp signal from an injury. C fibers are unmyelinated and much slower, carrying slow pain. A beta fibers are the large touch and vibration fibers, and B fibers are autonomic, so neither carries pain at all.

cards.q: Which fiber type carries slow pain?
cards.a: Unmyelinated C fibers.
options: Large myelinated A alpha fibers
Small myelinated A delta fibers
Unmyelinated C fibers
Large myelinated A beta fibers
cards.explanation: C fibers have no myelin, conduct at about 0.5 to 2 m/s, and produce the dull, aching pain that follows an injury and lingers. A delta fibers carry the sharp first pain. A alpha fibers serve proprioception from muscle and A beta fibers serve touch, and both are far too fast and too large to be the slow pain line.

cards.q: How would a patient describe fast pain?
cards.a: Sharp and easy to localize.
options: Dull and hard to localize
Sharp and easy to localize
Burning and slow to build
Cramping and spread over a wide area
cards.explanation: Fast pain arrives on A delta fibers with relatively little convergence in the cord, so it is felt as a sharp prick at a definite spot, which is the sensation that makes a person pull the hand back. Dull, burning, and diffuse descriptions all belong to slow pain on C fibers. The two qualities often follow one another from the same injury, which is why a single stimulus can be felt twice.

cards.q: How would a patient describe slow pain?
cards.a: Dull, aching or burning, and poorly localized.
options: Sharp and pinpointed to one spot
Brief and gone within a second
Felt only when the injured part is moved
Dull, aching or burning, and poorly localized
cards.explanation: Slow pain is carried by C fibers that converge heavily onto second order neurons, so the signal is smeared in space and the sensation is diffuse, aching, and persistent. Sharp and pinpointed describes fast pain on A delta fibers. Slow pain outlasts the stimulus rather than ending quickly, and it is present at rest rather than only on movement.

cards.q: What is referred pain?
cards.a: Pain from an internal organ that is felt in a surface region of the body.
options: Pain from an internal organ that is felt in a surface region of the body
Pain that spreads gradually to the surrounding skin as inflammation grows
Pain that persists after the injured tissue has fully healed
Pain that is felt on the side of the body opposite the injury
cards.explanation: Referred pain is a mislocalization: visceral afferents and somatic afferents converge on the same second order neurons, and the brain assigns the signal to the skin region it usually comes from. Spreading inflammation is a real process but it moves the actual source of the pain rather than misplacing it. Pain outlasting healing is chronic pain, and pain on the opposite side would indicate a central lesion.

cards.q: What anatomical arrangement explains referred pain?
cards.a: Visceral and somatic afferents converge onto the same second order neuron.
options: Visceral afferents cross the midline twice before reaching the thalamus
Visceral afferents travel in the dorsal columns rather than the spinothalamic tract
Visceral and somatic afferents converge onto the same second order neuron
Visceral afferents synapse directly in the thalamus with no spinal relay
cards.explanation: Because one dorsal horn neuron receives input from both the skin of a dermatome and a viscus that shares its spinal segment, activity on that neuron is ambiguous, and the brain interprets it according to the far more common source, which is skin. Visceral pain does travel in the spinothalamic system and does relay in the cord, so the other options misplace the pathway. The convergence itself, not the crossing pattern, is what produces the error.

cards.q: In the gate control theory, which afferent input closes the gate on pain transmission?
cards.a: Large diameter A beta touch fibers.
options: Additional C fiber input from the same region
Large diameter A beta touch fibers
Sympathetic postganglionic fibers
Second order spinothalamic axons
cards.explanation: Activity in large myelinated touch fibers excites inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, and those interneurons reduce transmission from nociceptive fibers to the projection neuron. More C fiber traffic opens the gate rather than closing it. Sympathetic fibers are motor to vessels and glands, and the spinothalamic axon is the output of the gate rather than an input to it.

cards.q: Which of these are endogenous opioids?
cards.a: Endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins.
options: Substance P, bradykinin, and histamine
Norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine
Glutamate, aspartate, and glycine
Endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins
cards.explanation: These three peptide families bind the same receptors that morphine binds and reduce pain transmission both in the dorsal horn and at higher levels. Substance P, bradykinin, and histamine work the other way, exciting or sensitizing nociceptors. Catecholamines and amino acid transmitters have many roles in the nervous system, but they are not the opioid peptides.

cards.q: Why is fast pain localized more precisely than slow pain?
cards.a: A delta fibers have smaller receptive fields and less convergence.
options: A delta fibers have smaller receptive fields and less convergence
A delta fibers travel in the dorsal columns, which preserve fine detail
A delta fibers are more numerous than C fibers in every tissue
A delta fibers fire at higher frequencies, which improves localization
cards.explanation: Localization is a spatial code, so it depends on how narrow each line is and how much information is thrown away at the first synapse, and the A delta system keeps both tighter than the C fiber system. Both pain fiber types ascend in the spinothalamic tract, not the dorsal columns. C fibers actually outnumber A delta fibers in most tissues, and firing rate carries intensity rather than position.

cards.q: A person stubs a toe and immediately rubs it, which lessens the pain. What is the mechanism?
cards.a: Touch input on A beta fibers drives interneurons that close the gate.
options: Rubbing warms the tissue and slows conduction in C fibers
Touch input on A beta fibers drives interneurons that close the gate
Rubbing releases endorphins from the skin into the local tissue
Rubbing physically shrinks the receptive fields of the nearby nociceptors
cards.explanation: Rubbing loads the large fiber touch system, and that traffic drives dorsal horn interneurons that inhibit transmission from nociceptors to the projection neuron, which is the everyday demonstration of gate control. A small change in skin temperature is not what does it. Endorphins act centrally rather than being released from skin, and receptive field size is anatomical and does not change with rubbing.

cards.q: During a heart attack, pain is often felt in the left arm and jaw rather than in the chest alone. Why?
cards.a: Cardiac afferents converge with somatic afferents in the same spinal segments.
options: The pain travels down the arm through the brachial plexus from the heart
Cardiac afferents cross to the left side and terminate in the arm area of cortex
Cardiac afferents converge with somatic afferents in the same spinal segments
Reduced cardiac output starves the arm muscles and causes them to ache
cards.explanation: Cardiac visceral afferents enter the cord around T1 to T5 and share second order neurons with skin and deep tissue of the left arm, shoulder, and jaw, so the brain refers the signal to the surface region it more often hears from. No nerve carries pain from the heart out into the arm. Cortical maps do not relabel a signal on their own, and arm muscle ischemia is not what makes the arm ache during a myocardial infarction.

cards.q: An investigator gives naloxone, which blocks opioid receptors, before a painful test. Stress induced analgesia largely disappears. What does that show?
cards.a: Endogenous opioids mediate a substantial part of that analgesia.
options: Pain fibers require opioid receptors in order to conduct at all
The dorsal horn gate depends entirely on large fiber touch input
Naloxone acts on the nociceptors in the skin to increase their firing
Endogenous opioids mediate a substantial part of that analgesia
cards.explanation: If blocking the receptors removes the effect, the effect was being produced by molecules acting at those receptors, which is a standard piece of pharmacological reasoning. Conduction in nociceptive fibers does not require opioid receptors and continues normally with naloxone present. Gate control by touch fibers is a separate mechanism that naloxone does not block, and naloxone works centrally rather than sensitizing skin receptors.

cards.q: A person steps on a sharp stone and feels a sharp pain almost immediately, then a dull ache about a second later. Why the delay between the two?
cards.a: C fibers conduct much more slowly than A delta fibers.
options: C fibers conduct much more slowly than A delta fibers
C fibers are activated only after inflammatory chemicals are released
The second pain travels a longer route through the brainstem
The thalamus deliberately delays the second signal to separate the two
cards.explanation: Both fiber types are activated by the same stone at the same instant, but unmyelinated C fibers conduct at around 1 m/s while myelinated A delta fibers conduct at ten or twenty times that, so from a foot the two arrivals are separated by about a second. Inflammatory chemicals do sensitize C fibers over minutes, but they are not needed for this first C fiber volley. Both pains share the spinothalamic route, and the thalamus does not insert delays.

cards.q: Stimulating the periaqueductal gray in the midbrain produces analgesia. How does an event in the midbrain reduce a signal entering at the spinal cord?
cards.a: It drives a descending pathway that inhibits transmission in the dorsal horn.
options: It raises the threshold of the nociceptors in the skin directly
It blocks conduction in the spinothalamic tract at the level of the pons
It drives a descending pathway that inhibits transmission in the dorsal horn
It prevents the thalamus from relaying any sensory signal to cortex
cards.explanation: The periaqueductal gray projects through the raphe nuclei to the dorsal horn, where released serotonin and enkephalin reduce transmitter release from nociceptive terminals and quiet the projection neuron, so the message is turned down at the first synapse. Central structures cannot reach out and change the threshold of a skin receptor. Nothing blocks the ascending tract in the pons, and thalamic relay of other modalities continues normally, since the analgesia is specific to pain.

cards.q: A patient has a neuropathy that has destroyed most A delta fibers in one leg while sparing C fibers. Predict what happens when that leg is pricked with a pin.
cards.a: The sharp first pain is missing, but a delayed dull ache still develops.
options: Neither the sharp pain nor the dull ache is felt
The sharp first pain is missing, but a delayed dull ache still develops
The sharp pain is felt normally, but no ache follows
Both pains are felt, but each arrives about a second later than normal
cards.explanation: A delta fibers carry the fast, sharp component and C fibers carry the slow, aching one, so losing one population removes one sensation and leaves the other intact. Total loss would require both populations to be gone. The sharp pain cannot be normal when its fibers are destroyed, and a uniform delay in both would suggest a general slowing rather than the selective loss described.

cards.q: A transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulator delivers a buzzing sensation over a painful area and reduces the pain while it runs. Which explanation fits the physiology?
cards.a: It recruits large A beta fibers, whose input closes the dorsal horn gate.
options: It fatigues the nociceptors in the skin until they stop transducing
It blocks conduction in C fibers by depolarizing them to inactivation
It stimulates the periaqueductal gray directly through the skin
It recruits large A beta fibers, whose input closes the dorsal horn gate
cards.explanation: Large myelinated fibers have the lowest electrical threshold, so a mild current recruits touch fibers first, which is why the sensation is a buzz rather than pain, and that touch traffic drives the inhibitory interneurons of the gate. Nociceptors do not fatigue in the way described, and a stimulus strong enough to inactivate C fibers would be intensely painful itself. Surface electrodes cannot reach a midbrain structure, though descending systems may add to the effect indirectly.

cards.q: After abdominal surgery, blood under the diaphragm irritates it and the patient reports pain at the top of the right shoulder. Work back from the finding to the mechanism.
cards.a: Phrenic afferents enter at C3 to C5 and converge with shoulder afferents.
options: Phrenic afferents enter at C3 to C5 and converge with shoulder afferents
Blood tracks up through the tissue planes and collects in the shoulder joint
The diaphragm and the shoulder share a single peripheral nerve trunk
Pain from the abdomen always refers upward because the spinothalamic tract ascends
cards.explanation: The diaphragm keeps the cervical innervation it had in the embryo, so its afferents arrive at spinal segments C3 to C5 and share second order neurons with the skin over the shoulder, and the brain assigns the signal to the shoulder. Blood does not travel to the shoulder joint, and the phrenic nerve is not shared with the shoulder skin, which is supplied by supraclavicular nerves from the same segments. Referral follows shared segments, not a general upward direction.

cards.q: A soldier with a serious leg wound continues to move to safety and reports almost no pain until an hour later. Which combination of mechanisms best explains this?
cards.a: Descending inhibition and endogenous opioids reduce dorsal horn transmission.
options: The nociceptors adapted quickly, so they stopped firing after the injury
Descending inhibition and endogenous opioids reduce dorsal horn transmission
The A delta and C fibers were severed, so no signal reached the cord
The thalamus stopped relaying all somatosensory input during the emergency itself
cards.explanation: Under extreme stress the periaqueductal gray and raphe system drive inhibition of the first pain synapse and opioid peptides are released, which turns the signal down before it ever ascends, and the pain returns as that drive falls off. Nociceptors adapt poorly, so peripheral adaptation cannot account for an hour of relief. Severed fibers would produce permanent numbness rather than delayed pain, and touch and position sense are unaffected, so a global thalamic shutdown is ruled out.

cards.q: Which instrument is used to measure two point discrimination in the lab?
cards.a: A two point caliper with an attached millimeter scale.
options: A tuning fork of known frequency
A two point caliper with an attached millimeter scale
A monofilament of calibrated bending force applied to the skin
A thermode set to a fixed temperature
cards.explanation: Two point discrimination is a distance measurement, so the tool must present two contacts a known number of millimeters apart, which is what the caliper or aesthesiometer does. A tuning fork tests vibration sense and a monofilament tests the force threshold for light touch, both useful but neither spatial. A thermode tests thermal thresholds and has nothing to do with spatial resolution.

cards.q: In a two point discrimination trial, what value is recorded as the threshold for that site?
cards.a: The smallest separation at which the subject reliably reports two points.
options: The smallest separation at which the subject reliably reports two points
The largest separation at which the subject still reports one point
The average of all separations tested at that site
The separation at which the subject first feels any contact at all
cards.explanation: The threshold is the boundary between one and two, and by convention it is reported as the smallest distance that is reliably resolved as two. The largest distance felt as one sits just below that boundary and is a different number. Averaging every separation tested measures nothing in particular, and the distance at which contact is first felt is a force threshold rather than a spatial one.

cards.q: Why are trials with only one caliper point randomly mixed into the series?
cards.a: To check that the subject is discriminating rather than guessing.
options: To let the skin recover between two point trials
To measure the subject's reaction time as a second dependent variable
To check that the subject is discriminating rather than guessing
To calibrate the caliper against a known separation
cards.explanation: A subject who says two on every trial will appear to have superb acuity unless the protocol can catch it, and single point catch trials do exactly that. Recovery time is handled by pacing the trials, not by changing the stimulus. Reaction time is not part of this measurement, and the caliper is calibrated against its own scale rather than against the subject.

cards.q: Why must both caliper points contact the skin at the same instant and with equal pressure?
cards.a: Staggered or unequal contact gives the subject a cue other than location.
options: Unequal pressure damages the receptors and raises the threshold permanently
Simultaneous contact is needed for the signals to reach the cortex together
Equal pressure keeps the caliper from bending and changing its separation
Staggered or unequal contact gives the subject a cue other than location
cards.explanation: The test is meant to isolate spatial resolution, so any other cue that reveals the presence of two contacts, such as one landing first or pressing harder, invalidates the measurement. Light caliper pressure does not damage receptors. Cortical arrival timing is not the issue, and a rigid caliper does not deform under the light forces used.

cards.q: In the coin demonstration of adaptation, what does the subject report?
cards.a: The sensation of the coin fades within a minute although it has not moved.
options: The sensation of the coin grows stronger as the skin warms
The sensation of the coin fades within a minute although it has not moved
The coin feels heavier the longer it rests on the skin
The coin is felt in a location a few centimeters away from where it rests
cards.explanation: Rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors stop firing during a steady, unchanging pressure, so the CNS receives no continuing touch signal and the coin drops out of awareness. A growing or heavier sensation would mean sensitization rather than adaptation. Mislocalization to a distant site describes referred sensation, which is a separate demonstration in this lab.

cards.q: In the lab demonstration of referred sensation, tapping the ulnar nerve where it crosses the elbow produces a sensation felt where?
cards.a: In the little finger and the ring finger.
options: In the little finger and the ring finger
At the elbow itself, where the tap was applied
In the thumb and the index finger
Diffusely over the whole forearm
cards.explanation: The ulnar nerve carries afferents from the medial hand, and stimulating those fibers anywhere along their length sends traffic on lines labeled for the little and ring fingers, so that is where the tingle is felt. Feeling it at the elbow would require the brain to track where along the axon the stimulus occurred, which it cannot do. The thumb and index finger are served by the median nerve, and the sensation is felt in a defined territory rather than diffusely.

cards.q: Why does the subject keep their eyes closed throughout the two point testing?
cards.a: Seeing the caliper would let the subject infer the answer.
options: Vision raises the firing rate of touch afferents
Closed eyes reduce the subject's overall skin temperature
Vision activates the same cortical region as touch
Seeing the caliper would let the subject infer the answer
cards.explanation: The measurement is a report of what the skin resolves, so any visual cue about how far apart the points are turns the trial into an inference rather than a discrimination. Vision does not change afferent firing or skin temperature. Visual and somatosensory cortex are distinct regions, so cortical overlap is not the concern here.

cards.q: In the adaptation demonstration, what quantity is actually recorded?
cards.a: The time from placement until the sensation disappears.
options: The mass of the object placed on the skin
The distance over which the sensation spreads across the skin
The time from placement until the sensation disappears
The number of receptors under the object
cards.explanation: Adaptation is a change over time, so the measured variable is how long the sensation persists before it fades, and comparing that time across sites or objects is what makes the demonstration quantitative. Mass is an independent variable the experimenter sets rather than the outcome. Spread of sensation and receptor counts cannot be measured with the equipment available in this lab.

cards.q: A subject reports two points on every trial, including the single point catch trials. What should you conclude?
cards.a: The data are unusable until the trials are repeated with better instruction.
options: The data are unusable until the trials are repeated with better instruction
The subject has unusually fine acuity at that site
The caliper must be out of calibration, since the points read too far apart
The subject's receptive fields at that site are unusually small
cards.explanation: Catch trials exist to detect exactly this pattern, and failing them means the responses are not tracking the stimulus, so any threshold computed from them is meaningless. Fine acuity would show up as correct discrimination at small separations along with correct single point reports. A caliper error would not make single points feel double, and small receptive fields cannot produce two sensations from one contact.

cards.q: Your group measures two point thresholds at the fingertip, the palm, the forearm, and the upper back. What order of thresholds should you predict from smallest to largest?
cards.a: Fingertip, palm, forearm, upper back.
options: Upper back, forearm, palm, fingertip
Fingertip, palm, forearm, upper back
Palm, fingertip, upper back, forearm
Forearm, palm, fingertip, upper back
cards.explanation: Threshold tracks receptor density and receptive field size, and those grade steadily from the densely innervated fingertip through the palm and forearm to the sparsely innervated back. The reversed order would put the coarsest surface first. Placing the palm ahead of the fingertip or the forearm last contradicts the innervation density of those sites, and the predicted ranking is what the lab data should reproduce.

cards.q: A student presses one caliper point noticeably harder than the other. How does that bias the measured threshold?
cards.a: It makes the threshold appear smaller, because the difference in pressure is an extra cue.
options: It makes the threshold appear larger, because the harder point masks the lighter one
It leaves the threshold unchanged, since only separation matters
It makes the threshold unmeasurable, because the skin will be damaged
It makes the threshold appear smaller, because the difference in pressure is an extra cue
cards.explanation: Two contacts of different strength feel different from a single contact even when both fall inside one receptive field, so the subject can call two at separations the skin cannot actually resolve and the threshold looks better than it is. Masking is not what happens, since both points are suprathreshold for detection. Separation is not the only thing the subject can use, which is the whole reason the protocol controls pressure, and the light forces involved cause no damage.

cards.q: A coin on the forearm has stopped being felt. A second coin is stacked on top of it and the sensation returns. Why?
cards.a: Adding weight changes the stimulus, and phasic receptors report change.
options: The second coin covers additional skin containing unadapted receptors
Adding weight changes the stimulus, and phasic receptors report change
The receptors under the first coin have finished recovering by then anyway
The added weight recruits nociceptors, which do not adapt
cards.explanation: Phasic receptors report transitions, so any change in the load, including an increase, produces a fresh burst of firing and a fresh sensation, which then fades again. The second coin sits on the first and covers roughly the same skin, so new territory is not the explanation. The adapted receptors have not recovered while the stimulus is still present, and the weight of a coin is nowhere near a noxious level.

cards.q: The ulnar nerve tap makes the little finger tingle even though nothing touched the finger. Which principle does the demonstration confirm?
cards.a: The labeled line principle, since sensation follows which fibers fire.
options: The labeled line principle, since sensation follows which fibers fire
Lateral inhibition, since the fingers on either side feel nothing at all
Adaptation, since the tingle fades quickly after the tap
Population coding, since many fibers are stimulated at once
cards.explanation: The stimulus is applied at the elbow and the sensation appears in the hand because those axons terminate centrally at the hand region of the map, which is the labeled line principle in its purest experimental form. Lateral inhibition sharpens borders and does not explain the mislocalization. The fading afterward and the number of fibers recruited are real but incidental to what this demonstration shows.

cards.q: A student records a two point threshold of 40 mm at the index fingertip. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.a: A procedural error, since fingertip thresholds are only a few mm.
options: The subject has an unusually dense fingertip innervation
A procedural error, since fingertip thresholds are only a few mm
The caliper was held perpendicular to the skin instead of at an angle
The subject adapted to the stimulus during the trial
cards.explanation: A value ten to twenty times the expected fingertip threshold points to how the measurement was made, most often the subject peeking, the points landing on the nail or on separate segments, or the series starting far too wide and never narrowing. Dense innervation would lower the number, not raise it. Perpendicular contact is the correct technique, and adaptation over a brief trial does not shift a spatial threshold this far.

cards.q: Why is each site tested several times rather than once, with the results averaged?
cards.a: Single trials are noisy, and averaging reduces the effect of a guess.
options: Repeated testing gradually lowers the threshold through practice
Repeated testing warms the skin and improves receptor function
Repeated testing is needed to fully adapt the receptors before measuring
Single trials are noisy, and averaging reduces the effect of a guess
cards.explanation: A two point judgment near threshold is probabilistic, so any one trial may land either way, and several trials give a more stable estimate of where the boundary actually sits. Practice effects and skin warming are confounds to be avoided rather than reasons to repeat. Deliberately adapting the receptors before measuring would corrupt the measurement, since adapted receptors report less.

cards.q: A lab group reports these thresholds: fingertip 3 mm, palm 11 mm, forearm 38 mm, back 52 mm. What can they conclude about receptive fields and cortical territory across the four sites?
cards.a: Receptive fields grow from fingertip to back, while cortical territory per unit of skin falls.
options: Receptive fields grow from fingertip to back, and cortical territory per unit of skin grows with them
Receptive fields shrink from fingertip to back, while cortical territory per unit of skin grows
Receptive fields grow from fingertip to back, while cortical territory per unit of skin falls
Receptive fields are the same at all four sites, and only cortical territory differs
cards.explanation: A rising threshold means larger, more overlapping receptive fields, and fewer separate lines coming from a given area of skin means less cortex is needed to keep them apart, so the two measures move in opposite directions across the four sites. Fields and cortical territory cannot both grow, since dense innervation is what produces both small fields and a large cortical strip. Equal fields could not produce a seventeenfold spread in threshold.

cards.q: A classmate says the coin sensation faded only because the subject got bored and stopped paying attention. How would you modify the demonstration to test that claim?
cards.a: Slide the coin slightly at a random moment and see whether sensation returns.
options: Slide the coin slightly at a random moment and see whether sensation returns
Ask the subject to concentrate harder on the coin for the whole trial period
Repeat the trial with a heavier coin and time the fade again
Test a second subject and compare their fade times
cards.explanation: If attention were the explanation, moving the coin should change nothing, but if peripheral adaptation is the explanation, any change in the stimulus reactivates the phasic receptors and the sensation snaps back at once, which separates the two accounts cleanly. Instructing the subject to concentrate cannot be verified and does not distinguish the hypotheses. A heavier coin or a second subject changes the conditions without addressing whether the fade is peripheral or central.

cards.q: A group reports identical two point thresholds of 25 mm at the fingertip and the palm. Which methodological error best explains this result?
cards.a: The series never narrowed below 25 mm, so the true threshold was missed.
options: The subject's eyes were closed, hiding the caliper from view
The caliper points were applied simultaneously and with equal pressure
Single point catch trials were included in the series
The series never narrowed below 25 mm, so the true threshold was missed
cards.explanation: A fingertip threshold near 3 mm can only be found by testing separations down in that range, and a series that stops at 25 mm will return 25 mm for any site whose true threshold is smaller, flattening the real differences. Closed eyes, simultaneous equal pressure, and catch trials are all correct procedure and would improve the data rather than distort it. When two very different sites give the same number, suspect a floor in the protocol before suspecting the physiology.

cards.q: You want to show that a referred sensation really comes from stimulating the nerve trunk and not from the skin over the elbow. What control belongs in the design?
cards.a: Tap nearby skin away from the nerve with equal force and note where it is felt.
options: Tap the ulnar nerve harder and record whether the tingle grows
Tap nearby skin away from the nerve with equal force and note where it is felt
Tap the little finger directly and record whether it is felt there
Repeat the tap after the subject has adapted to a coin resting on the forearm skin
cards.explanation: The control has to hold the stimulus constant and change only whether the nerve trunk is under the point of contact, so an equally firm tap on nearby skin should be felt locally at the elbow if the nerve is what produces the referral. Tapping harder varies intensity rather than testing the hypothesis. Tapping the finger tests nothing that is in doubt, and an unrelated adaptation trial does not bear on where the sensation is assigned.
